extracted.intended_audience: advanced high-school / undergraduate mathematics students (readers of Evan Chen's Napkin notes), especially those learning algebraic topology/group theory and measure theory
extracted.subtask_description: Two connected textbook-scale subtasks: (1) a topological/group-theoretic explanation of why there is no general quintic formula (Abel–Ruffini style/topological proof), and (2) the definitions and basic constructions of measure spaces, pre-measures, outer measures, and the Lebesgue measure. Targets readers learning the formal definitions and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Quintic formula
rubrics_metrics.description: A quintic formula would be a formula taking in the coefficients (a0, ..., a5) of a degree 5 polynomial P, using the operations +, −, ×, ÷, n-th root finitely many times, that maps to the five roots (z1, · · · , z5) of P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the formal object that the topological Abel–Ruffini argument aims to rule out; later remarks note that allowing more complicated functions (e.g., Bring radicals) changes what is considered 'fair game'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity / root-tracking requirement for any formula F
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proposed quintic formula F receives the same coefficients when the roots are permuted continuously, and thus must produce outputs that track which root is which when moving roots along smooth paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 34.1.2 invites the reader to convince themselves that F must track root identity along smooth deformations. This continuity/tracking constraint is the key obstruction used in the topological argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstruction via permutation by continuous deformation (rational selector argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rational function R always finds a root of a quintic P(z) = ∏(z − zi) and R is continuous, then smoothly swapping two roots along non-intersecting paths that avoid other roots yields the same coefficients but forces R to change output, a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the simplest obstruction (ignoring n-th root operations): continuity of a root-selector combined with nontrivial permutations of roots (monodromy) can contradict single-valuedness of R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a nested radical
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of a nested radical is defined as the maximum number of times radicals can be found in other radicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to formalize the complexity of expressions built from nested n-th roots (e.g., quadratic, cubic formulas), and to reason about how commutators can be iterated to handle nested phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling phases with commutators for nested radicals
rubrics_metrics.description: When n-th roots (radicals) are allowed, individual swaps of roots can accumulate phase changes (abelian data) that prevent direct contradiction; taking commutators of swaps can fix phase changes while producing a nontrivial permutation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the quadratic formula (square-root branches swapping) and cubic formula (nested radicals). The idea is to combine swaps (and nested commutators) so that phase effects cancel but nonabelian permutation effects remain, obstructing any formula built from finitely many nested radicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derived series and commutator chain (group-theoretic reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the chain S5 = G ⊇ G(1) ⊇ G(2) ⊇ ... where each group is the commutator subgroup of the previous (the derived series); the argument reduces to showing this derived series never becomes trivial in the allowed operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 34.4.1 and Definition 34.4.2 discuss properties of commutator subgroups and the notion of solvability. The goal is to show S5 (or A5) is not solvable to conclude no universal formula exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Solvable group (as stated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition as given: 'A group G is solvable if its derived series is nontrivial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the textbook's presented definition context for the chapter; the derived series G ⊇ [G,G] ⊇ [ [G,G], [G,G] ] ⊇ ... is central. (Readers should note standard alternative phrasing: solvable groups are those whose derived series reaches the trivial group after finitely many steps.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary / scope of topological Abel–Ruffini argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument shows there is no formula that works for all degree 5 polynomials (i.e., no single expression using the allowed operations that outputs the roots for every quintic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Con: it doesn't exhibit a specific quintic whose roots cannot be expressed; Pro: the argument is robust to adding many elementary functions (exp, sin, cos) and connects to the non-solvability of A5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter/notation connotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventions for letters used in the measure-theory chapters: measure spaces denoted by Ω with elements ω; algebras/σ-algebras by script A,B; measurable sets by capital Roman A,B,C,...; measures by µ or ρ; random variables by X,Y,Z; functions R→R by Roman letters f,g for pdfs and F,G for cdfs; real numbers by x,y,z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a notational rubric intended to help the reader quickly infer the 'type' of an object from its letter—useful for reading subsequent sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Measurable space / σ-algebra (axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A measurable space consists of a set Ω and a σ-algebra A of subsets of Ω. The σ-algebra A is required to: (i) contain ∅ and Ω, and (ii) be closed under complements and countable unions/intersections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate minimal axiom noted: closure under complements and countable unions suffices (intersections follow by De Morgan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: σ-algebra generated by a family F
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a family F of subsets of Ω, the σ-algebra generated by F is the smallest σ-algebra A which contains F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically this is described as 'start with F (e.g., open sets) and close under complements and countable unions'; explicit constructions may require transfinite induction but generation is how one usually reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: Power set σ-algebra (2^Ω)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is any set, the power set A = 2^Ω is a σ-algebra (contains all subsets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used when Ω is finite or countable; trivial but often unhelpful when Ω is large/uncontrollable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: Countable / co-countable σ-algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is uncountable, one can take A to be the family of subsets that are either countable or have countable complement; this family is a σ-algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This σ-algebra is coarse and demonstrates extreme examples of σ-algebras on uncountable sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: Borel σ-algebra and Borel space
rubrics_metrics.description: For a topological space Ω, the Borel σ-algebra B(Ω) is the σ-algebra generated by open sets. The pair (Ω, B(Ω)) is called a Borel space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: B(Ω) is usually impossible to describe element-by-element; think of it as 'everything you can make from open sets by countable unions, complements, etc.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Measure and measure space (axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure µ : A → [0, +∞] on a σ-algebra A must satisfy µ(∅)=0 and countable additivity: for disjoint An in A, µ(⋃n An) = Σn µ(An). The triple (Ω, A, µ) is a measure space; it is a probability space if µ(Ω)=1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing +∞ in the codomain permits general measures; many concrete results require only σ-additivity and µ(∅)=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaker / equivalent axioms for A and µ
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative minimal axioms: (a) For A: ∅∈A and closure under complements and countable unions; (b) For µ: µ(∅)=0, finite additivity µ(A⊔B)=µ(A)+µ(B), and continuity from above for decreasing sequences with finite measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These variants are useful when proving a candidate is a σ-algebra or a measure with less checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity of measure (consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A ⊆ B are measurable, then µ(A) ≤ µ(B), since µ(B) = µ(A) + µ(B	ext{A}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an immediate and frequently used consequence of countable additivity and nonnegativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: Counting measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Define µ(A) = |A| for A ∈ A (possibly ∞); this is a measure (counting measure). Often normalized by µ(A) = |A|/|Ω| to make a probability space when Ω is finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the canonical discrete measure and is useful intuition for probability on countable sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: Measure on countable/co-countable σ-algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: On the σ-algebra of countable or co-countable subsets, define µ(A)=0 if A is countable, and µ(A)=1 if its complement is countable; this defines a measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a concrete nontrivial measure on an uncountable set with a very coarse σ-algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitali / Banach–Tarski style obstruction to measuring all subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no way to assign a translation/rotation-invariant 'volume' to every subset of R^n while preserving basic sanity checks. For example, partitioning the unit circle into equivalence classes under rational rotations and choosing representatives leads to a set X where assigning a consistent measure to all rotations of X forces a contradiction (either total measure 0 or ∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows why one must restrict to 'measurable' sets (e.g., Borel or Lebesgue measurable) rather than attempting to measure 2^Ω.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Measurable function
rubrics_metrics.description: Given measurable spaces (X, A) and (Y, B), a function f:X→Y is measurable if for any S∈B the preimage f^{-1}(S) ∈ A. When Y is R with the Borel σ-algebra, it suffices to check preimages of open sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For nonnegative f, measurability is the exact condition needed so that the Lebesgue integral ∫_Ω f dµ exists; continuity implies Borel measurability (Proposition 35.7.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: Continuous ⇒ Borel measurable
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y are topological spaces with Borel σ-algebras, any continuous f:X→Y is measurable (preimages of open sets are open and thus Borel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies that most familiar continuous functions encountered are measurable in the Borel sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: 'Almost everywhere' / 'almost surely'
rubrics_metrics.description: A property P holds almost everywhere (or almost surely) if the set {ω ∈ Ω | P does not hold for ω} has measure zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure-theoretic statements typically regard functions/equalities up to measure-zero differences; uniqueness results are often only up to null sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Algebra (for pre-measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: An algebra A0 on Ω is a nonempty subset of 2^Ω closed under complements and finite unions. The smallest algebra containing a family F is the algebra generated by F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebras weaken σ-algebras by replacing 'countable' with 'finite'—they are the natural domain for defining pre-measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Pre-measure
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-measure µ0 on an algebra A0 is a function µ0 : A0 → [0, +∞] satisfying µ0(∅)=0 and countable additivity for any disjoint sequence A1,A2,... in A0 provided the union ⋃n An is also in A0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-measures are the starting point for constructing outer measures and ultimately full measures via Carathéodory extension; geometric intuition (e.g., area of rectangles) is often used to define µ0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Outer measure (axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: An outer measure µ* : 2^Ω → [0, +∞] satisfies µ*(∅)=0, monotonicity (E⊆F ⇒ µ*(E)≤µ*(F)), and countable subadditivity µ*(⋃n En) ≤ Σn µ*(En) for any sequence of subsets En.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outer measures are typically obtained by approximating sets from outside (coverings); they are not full measures but are the intermediate object in Carathéodory's construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction: Outer measure from a pre-measure (Theorem 36.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a pre-measure µ0 on an algebra A0, define µ*(E) = inf { Σn µ0(An) | An ∈ A0, E ⊆ ⋃n An }. Then µ* is an outer measure and µ*(A)=µ0(A) for all A∈A0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: µ*(E) is the infimum of µ0-measures of countable coverings of E by sets from A0. Part (b) guarantees compatibility on the initial algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carathéodory measurability criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is µ*-measurable (Carathéodory measurable) if for every E ⊆ Ω, µ*(E) = µ*(E ∩ A) + µ*(E  ackslash A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition identifies the σ-algebra of sets on which the restricted µ* will be a proper measure; it has geometric interpretations in R^n (see Proposition 36.4.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility: initial algebra contained in Carathéodory measurable sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If µ* is obtained from a pre-measure µ0 on an algebra A0, then every set in A0 is µ*-measurable (Proposition 36.3.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the second half of the compatibility that ensures the final measure extends the pre-measure on the original algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Null set and completeness of a measure space
rubrics_metrics.description: A null set is A ∈ A with µ(A)=0. A measure space (Ω, A, µ) is complete if every subset of a null set is measurable (hence null).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness is desirable because once a set is measured zero, any of its subsets should also be measurable and assigned measure zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carathéodory extension theorem (for outer measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: If µ* is an outer measure and A_cm is the collection of µ*-measurable sets, then A_cm is a σ-algebra and the restriction µ_cm of µ* to A_cm gives a complete measure space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composing the outer-measure-from-pre-measure construction with Carathéodory extension yields a complete measure that extends the original pre-measure (compatibility results ensure agreement on A0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction steps for the Lebesgue measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Create Lebesgue measure λ on R^n by: (1) start with algebra L0 generated by rectangular prisms and define a pre-measure λ0 (rectangle volumes); (2) form Lebesgue outer measure λ* from λ0 via infimum of coverings; (3) restrict λ* to the σ-algebra L(R^n) of λ*-measurable sets (Carathéodory) to obtain the complete Lebesgue measure λ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resulting σ-algebra L(R^n) (Lebesgue σ-algebra) contains all rectangles and is complete. After construction, computations use the measure's properties rather than the construction details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: Cantor set has Lebesgue measure zero
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle-thirds Cantor set C ⊆ [0,1] is measurable and µ(C)=0 because at the nth step the remaining set has length (2/3)^n, so µ(C) ≤ (2/3)^n for all n, forcing µ(C)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This example illustrates sets that are uncountable yet of measure zero and demonstrates practical consequences of the Lebesgue measure construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat about overly general outer-measure generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although for any ρ defined on some family E one can define µ*(E) = inf Σ ρ(En) over coverings to get an outer measure, this construction is often too general and may not guarantee compatibility with ρ; better to apply the construction starting from a pre-measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that one should ensure sanity conditions on the initial function (preferably a pre-measure) so that the resulting outer measure behaves as intended and matches the initial data on the generating algebra.
